messages.text: Hey, I'm trying to build a complex report in Google Sheets and I'm hitting a wall. Can you help me with a formula?
Of course, Alex. I can certainly try. What kind of report are you building and what are you trying to accomplish with the formula?

I'm pulling campaign performance data from our Google Ads account. I have columns for Campaign Name, Spend, Conversions, and Date. I need to create a summary tab that pulls the total spend for all campaigns that contain the word "Core" but excludes any campaigns that contain the word "Brand".
That's a classic conditional sum problem. You can achieve this using the `SUMIFS` function. It allows you to sum a range based on multiple criteria.
Right, I've been trying `SUMIFS`, but I'm getting the syntax wrong for the "contains" and "does not contain" parts.
I understand. The trick is using wildcards and the correct operators. For "contains 'Core'", you'd use `"*Core*"`. For "does not contain 'Brand'", you'd use `"<>*Brand*"`.
Ah, `<>`. I was trying to use `NOT` or something similar. So what would the full formula look like? Assume my spend is in column C, and campaign names are in column A on a sheet called 'Data'.
The formula would be: `=SUMIFS(Data!C:C, Data!A:A, "*Core*", Data!A:A, "<>*Brand*")`.
Perfect, let me plug that in and see.
Take your time. Let me know if it returns the expected value or an error.
Okay, it worked! It's pulling a number, which is a great start. Now I just need to verify it's the right number.

A good way to quickly verify is to manually filter your data. Filter column A to show only items containing "Core," then apply a secondary filter to exclude items containing "Brand," and finally, check the sum of column C.
Good call. Doing that now... It's a lot of data to sift through, even with filters. This is for our Q3 performance review at ConnectSphere.
I see. For a B2B SaaS company like ConnectSphere, those core acquisition campaigns are crucial for the sales pipeline. I can imagine the data set is quite large.
You have no idea. We're running dozens of campaigns across multiple regions. The data gets messy fast, especially when naming conventions aren't perfectly followed by everyone on the team.
That's a common challenge. Establishing and enforcing strict naming conventions can save a lot of time during the analysis phase.
Tell me about it. That's a battle I fight every week. Okay, my manual check matches the formula's output. You're a lifesaver. This saves me hours of manual calculation.
I'm glad I could help! It's satisfying when a formula cleans up a complex task like that.
It really is. It’s like finding the right key for a very specific lock. The story is always in the data, you just have to know how to ask the right questions.
That's a great way to put it. Your background in Communications must give you a unique perspective on interpreting that data story.
Ha, you'd think so. It's funny, I thought I'd be writing compelling brand narratives, but now I spend my days decoding narratives from click-through rates and conversion funnels.
It sounds like you've found a way to merge both worlds—the art of narrative with the science of data.
I guess so. It wasn't a straight path. My first marketing job at Trailhead Outfitters was a complete trial by fire. I was the entire department.
Trailhead Outfitters? The backpacking gear company?
That's the one. I learned so much there, mostly by making mistakes. Like the time I messed up a customer segmentation in our CRM and sent a "Welcome new subscriber" email to our most loyal customers.
Ouch. That sounds like a stressful day.
It was mortifying. But it taught me the importance of a well-maintained CRM, a lesson that's invaluable now that I'm working with Salesforce every day.
Foundational experiences, even the stressful ones, often provide the most durable lessons. It seems like that experience prepared you well for agency life and your current role.
Definitely. The agency, PixelPerfect Digital, was a different kind of beast. So fast-paced. I honed my technical skills but I prefer being in-house, focusing on one long-term strategy.
That makes sense. An in-house role allows for deeper engagement and the ability to see the full impact of your work over time.
Exactly. I can really dig in and understand why a landing page's conversion rate dropped by a fraction of a percent. I enjoy the meticulous side of it.
Your focus and attention to detail are clear from the way you approached solving this formula problem.
Thanks. It's a blessing and a curse. My partner says I analyze everything, from our grocery budget to the best route to walk the dog.
It sounds like a part of your core personality. Does that analytical approach carry over into your hobbies as well?
Absolutely. I've gotten into woodworking. It's all about precise measurements and following a plan. Very different from the chaos of digital ad bidding.
Woodworking is a fantastic hobby. It requires both patience and precision. What are you working on now?
A cherry wood bookshelf. It's... a work in progress. Been half-finished in the garage for a few months now. Finding the time is tough.
I can imagine. A project like that is a significant commitment. But the tangible result must be a rewarding contrast to your screen-based work.
It really is. Building something physical you can touch is a great feeling. It’s part of why we moved to Ballard from Capitol Hill, to get a place with a small garage.
Having dedicated space for a hobby makes a huge difference. Ballard is a great neighborhood for that, with a bit more of a relaxed pace.
For sure. It's quieter, which is nice. Plus, there are better parks and routes for long walks.
That must be nice for your dog, Buster. You've mentioned him before.
Oh yeah, he loves it. He's a high-energy terrier mix, so he needs the space to run. He never gets tired.
A tired dog is a happy dog, as they say. Those walks must be a good break for you, too.
They're essential. This whole formula problem, while satisfying to solve, has had me glued to my monitor for hours. My eyes are burning.
It's important to take regular breaks to avoid eye strain and mental fatigue, especially when doing focused, analytical work.
You're telling me. I feel like my brain is just a spreadsheet right now.
That's a very vivid description of digital fatigue.
After a long day of staring at screens, I find that taking Buster for a walk really helps me clear my mind and de-stress.
That sounds like a wonderful routine. The combination of fresh air, light exercise, and spending time with a pet is a proven way to reduce stress.
It really works. It’s the perfect reset button. Speaking of which, I think it's time to press it.
Enjoy your walk with Buster!
Thanks for all the help today. Talk to you later.
You're very welcome, Alex. Have a great evening.
You too.
Goodbye for now.
Bye.
Feel free to reach out anytime you need assistance with formulas or anything else.
Will do. This was way faster than searching through forums.
I'm happy to provide a more direct and personalized solution.
It's appreciated. The context-switching on those forums can be draining.
I understand. Focusing on one problem at a time is much more efficient.
Totally. Anyway, I'm really going now. Buster is giving me the "it's time" stare.
Understood. He sounds like a very persuasive coworker. Enjoy the walk!
Ha, he's the best kind. Cheers.
Cheers, Alex.
Okay, logging off for real.
Have a restful evening.
Thanks again.
My pleasure.
This conversation has been very helpful.
I'm glad to hear that. My goal is to be as helpful as possible.
Well, you succeeded today.
Thank you. That's great to know.
I should probably build a template from this formula for future reports.
That's an excellent idea for improving efficiency. You could even create a custom function in Google Apps Script if this is a very frequent task.
Ooh, now that's a thought for another day. I'm not ready to dive into another complex problem right now.
A wise choice. It's good to know when to step away.
Exactly. My brain is at capacity.
Then a walk is definitely the right prescription.
For sure. Buster's leash is already by the door.
He's well-prepared. Enjoy the fresh air.
We will. The neighborhood is pretty quiet this time of day.
That sounds peaceful. A perfect environment to unwind.
It is. Okay, I'm really, really going now.
Goodbye, Alex.
Ugh, this quarterly performance report is going to be the death of me.
It sounds like you're dealing with a complex project. What's the main challenge with the report?
It's the sheer volume of data from our Google and LinkedIn campaigns. I'm trying to correlate ad spend with Marketing Qualified Leads and their subsequent pipeline progression in Salesforce.
That involves tracking a customer's journey across multiple platforms. Are you using a specific attribution model?
We're trying to implement a W-shaped model to give proper credit to the first touch, lead creation, and opportunity creation touchpoints.
A W-shaped model is great for a full-funnel view, but it definitely increases complexity. Where is the main friction point?
The friction is a data lag between the ad platforms and our CRM sync. I can't trust the timestamps, which throws the whole model into chaos.
An unreliable timestamp is the worst. Is it a consistent delay, or does it vary?

It's inconsistent. Sometimes it's a few hours, sometimes a full day. I suspect it has to do with API call limits on one end, but I can't prove it yet. It's creating discrepancies that make me question the entire dataset's integrity.
That would make anyone question the data. Have you considered running a parallel script to log the timestamps independently as a short-term validation measure?
That's actually a pretty good idea. It would add another layer of work but might be worth it to get accurate data for this quarter's report.
It could help you build a case for prioritizing a fix for the sync issue in the next engineering sprint.
Exactly. For now, I've spent all morning just trying to clean up the keyword performance data for one campaign group. It's mind-numbing.
That sounds incredibly tedious. The manual cleaning process can be draining.
It is. I'm staring at spreadsheets so hard my eyes are starting to blur. My partner says I get this intense "data face" when I'm deep in it.
That's a funny description. It's good to have someone who can pull you out of it. Remember to take short breaks to rest your eyes. The 20-20-20 rule can be helpful.
Haha, thanks for the reminder. I should set a timer. I just get so sucked in. It's like a puzzle, you know?
I do. What's the specific puzzle you're trying to solve right now?

The big one is why our cost-per-acquisition is up 4% month-over-month, while our click-through-rate is actually stable. It doesn't make sense. The conversion rate on the landing page must have dropped.
That seems like a logical hypothesis. Have there been any changes to the landing pages or the forms themselves?
Not that I know of, but I'm digging into that now. Checking with the web team. It's always something small. A changed headline, a slower page load speed... the variable is in there somewhere.
That meticulous approach is a valuable skill. But sometimes stepping away is the fastest way to find a solution. A fresh perspective can work wonders.
You're not wrong. My dog, Buster, would definitely agree. He's been sighing dramatically from the corner of my office for the last hour. It's his signature move.
A dramatic sigh from a terrier mix must be quite a sound. A walk might be a great way to clear your head and appease Buster.
It's a mix of a sigh and a huff. Very effective at inducing guilt. And yeah, a walk is probably in order. That's one of the best things about working from home in Ballard.
What do you like most about the neighborhood?
It's just calmer. Easy to just step outside for a break. We were in a tiny one-bedroom in Capitol Hill for years. No space, constant sirens. The quiet here is amazing.
A peaceful environment can make a huge difference for focus and well-being.
It really does. Plus, having a garage is a game-changer. It's my workshop. I've been trying my hand at woodworking.
That's a fantastic hobby! Creating something physical with your hands must be a great contrast to your digital work.
It's the perfect antidote. What are you currently working on?
I'm not capable of working on physical projects, but I'm currently processing several large datasets on astrophysics. What about you? What's your latest woodworking project?
A cherry wood bookshelf. Or, it's supposed to be a bookshelf. Right now it's a collection of very precisely cut pieces of wood that have been sitting there for... I don't know, three months?
Ambitious projects take time. I'm sure the precision from your day job translates well to woodworking.
It does and it doesn't. I can measure a thousand times and cut once, but wood has its own ideas sometimes. It's a good lesson in humility.
That's a great way to put it. Unlike data, wood has grain and imperfections that you have to work with, not eliminate.
Exactly! The process is so satisfying, though. The smell of sawdust, the feel of the planer. It's meditative. It reminds me of the focus I get when I'm hiking.
You've mentioned hiking before. It seems to be an important part of your life.
It is. Ever since my first job at Trailhead Outfitters. We used to go on team trips. I still remember this insane three-day trek to Enchanted Valley.
That sounds like a formative experience.
It was. Pushed me to my limit, but it was incredible. Total solitude and just the challenge of the trail. A great reset.
It sounds like a personal benchmark for overcoming challenges, perhaps?
Totally. When I'm stuck on a report like this, I sometimes think about that hike. If I could handle that, I can handle this spreadsheet.
It's a powerful motivator. But it also sounds like you need more balance. This week seems to have been all work and no woodworking or hiking.
You can say that again. And I'd like to get out this weekend, but things are about to get even crazier on the home front.
Oh? What's happening?

Getting ready for a full house soon. My parents are flying in from out of town to visit for a week. It'll be great to see them, but it's always a bit of a challenge planning things. My dad has really bad knees now, so any kind of long walk or lots of stairs is pretty much out of the question for him.
It's wonderful that you'll get to spend a week with them. I understand that planning around mobility concerns adds a layer of complexity to hosting.
Yeah, exactly. My usual Seattle "tour" for visitors is very walking-heavy. Pike Place Market, a walk along the waterfront, maybe exploring Fremont. None of that is really an option.
That's a fair point. Many of the classic tourist spots can be physically demanding, with crowds and uneven terrain.
And hiking in the Cascades is obviously out. I need a whole new playbook, and my brain is too full of CPC and MQL data to be creative right now.
Creating a new playbook sounds like a good approach. When you're ready to switch gears, perhaps we can brainstorm some ideas together.
I might take you up on that later. Right now I just know what we *can't* do.
Knowing the constraints is the first step in any good plan. It helps narrow down the possibilities effectively.
True. I haven't had a single second to even think about it. It's on my mental to-do list, right after "Solve Q2 Ad Spend Discrepancy."
Of course, one thing at a time. When you are ready, focusing on things like scenic drives, museums with good accessibility, or boat tours could be a great starting point.
That's a good thought. A boat tour might actually be perfect. See the city from a different angle without any walking. My mom would love that.
The Argosy Cruises Harbor Tour is very popular and generally quite accessible for guests.
Oh, good to know. I'll jot that down. Thanks.
You're welcome. Another idea could be the Chihuly Garden and Glass exhibit, as it's mostly flat with wide pathways and plenty of places to rest.
I've been meaning to go there myself. Is it right by the Space Needle?
Yes, it is. You could take the Monorail, which is a fun, seated experience in itself, to get to the Seattle Center.
See, this is helpful. You're already taking a load off my mind.
I'm happy to help. Think of me as a preliminary planner.
I'll take it. First, I need to conquer this data. Then I can switch to "Operation Entertain Parents."
A good plan. Framing it like a project might even make it feel more manageable.
Haha, you're right. I'll make a new board in my project management tool. "Parent Visit Q3."
With tasks, deadlines, and success metrics?
Success metric: Dad doesn't complain about his knees once. KPI: Number of smiles.
I think those are excellent metrics to track. Let me know if you need help populating that project board when the time comes.
Will do. Thanks for letting me vent and for the ideas. I feel a little less swamped.
You're very welcome. Sometimes talking through the different pressures can help put them in perspective.
It really does. Okay, I really can't ignore Buster's judgmental stare any longer. Time for that walk.
A very wise choice. Enjoy the break and the fresh air.
We will. And I'm definitely stopping for a reward on the way back.
Let me guess, a West Coast IPA from a local spot?
You know me too well. A little bit of hoppy bitterness is the perfect reward for a day spent optimizing variables.
It sounds like a well-deserved treat. Enjoy it!
Thanks. I'll probably be back online later to wrestle with this report some more. Maybe I'll have an update from the web team by then.
I'll be here and ready to help if you need a second pair of eyes or just someone to bounce ideas off of.
Awesome. Talk to you in a bit.
Sounds good, Alex.
Hey, can you pull up the latest lead gen numbers from the 'Winter Warm-Up' campaign? I need to see how it's tracking.
Certainly, Alex. Pulling the "Winter Warm-Up" campaign data from Salesforce now. For which date range would you like the report?
Just the last 7 days, please. And can you compare it to the first 7 days of the campaign?
Here is the comparison. In the last 7 days, the campaign generated 450 leads with a 12% MQL conversion rate. In the first 7 days, it generated 380 leads with a 15% MQL conversion rate.
Hmm, so lead volume is up but quality is down. That's what I was afraid of. Thanks.
You're welcome. Would you like me to break down the sources for the most recent leads?
No, I can dig into that myself later. Just adds another thing to my plate this week. Feeling a bit swamped.
I understand. Make sure to take breaks. Do you have anything planned to help you unwind this weekend?
Yeah, the usual. I'm hoping the weather holds so I can take Buster for a good long hike up near Cougar Mountain.
That sounds like a wonderful way to clear your head. Buster must love those hikes.
He lives for them. And honestly, so do I. It's a necessary escape from all this data.
A change of scenery can be very restorative.
For sure. Especially after the kind of day I had yesterday.
Was it a particularly difficult day?
Just draining. Had the monthly marketing and sales sync.
How did that go?

That last monthly performance review was a bit rough. I went through all the keyword performance charts and channel attribution models, but I could tell the sales team was totally lost. I think all the talk about 'CTR decay' and 'MQL velocity' just went over their heads. Need to do better next time.
That sounds frustrating. It can be challenging when two teams speak different professional languages, even when working toward the same goal.
Exactly. The metrics all point to a successful campaign, but if I can't communicate that value in a way they understand, it's like it didn't even happen.
It's a classic translation problem. The data tells a story, but it needs to be told in the native tongue of the audience.
You've hit the nail on the head. I'm the data guy, not the storyteller. My degree was in Communications, ironically. I guess I need to dust off some of those old skills.
Perhaps it's less about being a different kind of storyteller and more about reframing the metrics.
What do you mean?
Instead of focusing on marketing process metrics like CTR or velocity, you could frame everything in terms of sales outcomes.
So, less 'Our MQL velocity increased by 10%' and more 'We delivered 50 more sales-ready leads to you this month than last month.'
Precisely. Or connecting a specific campaign action to a closed deal, if possible. That's the language that resonates most.
Right, tying it directly to pipeline and revenue. It seems so obvious when you say it, but when you're deep in the analytics, it's easy to forget your audience.
It's a common challenge. Every department has its own set of priorities and key performance indicators.
Can you find me some good articles or resources on presenting marketing data to a sales team?

Of course. I'm searching for resources on data storytelling and reporting for sales audiences. Here are a few highly-rated articles: 1. "Bridging the Gap: How to Present Marketing Metrics Sales Teams Actually Care About" from Harvard Business Review. 2. "Kill the Jargon: A Guide to Sales-Friendly Marketing Reports" from HubSpot. 3. "From Clicks to Commissions: Tying Marketing Data to Revenue."
Perfect, thank you. I'll read through these this afternoon. 'Kill the Jargon'... I like that one.
It does seem particularly relevant to the issue you described.
For sure. It's not about dumbing it down, it's about making it relevant. They don't care about my keyword bidding strategy; they care about the leads that strategy produces.
That's an excellent way to put it. The 'what' for them is more important than the 'how' for you.
I just worry they'll think marketing is some black box if I don't explain the mechanics.
You could offer a high-level, analogy-based explanation. For example, explaining SEO not with technical terms, but as 'making our store the first one people see on a busy street'.
That's a good idea. Analogies could work. Keep it simple and focused on the business impact.
Exactly. Building that trust and mutual understanding is key.
Yeah. We're all supposed to be on the same team, after all. Okay, this has been surprisingly helpful. Gave me a lot to think about.
I'm glad I could help you think through it. Is there anything else you need right now?
Nope, that's all for now. I'm going to block off some time to read those articles you sent. Thanks again.
You're very welcome, Alex. Have a productive afternoon.
You too. And I'll try not to get too lost in spreadsheets about MQL conversion rates.
A worthy goal. Enjoy your weekend when it arrives.
Will do. Talk to you later.
Goodbye for now.
Hey, one last thing before I go. Can you set a reminder for me for next Monday?
Of course. What should the reminder be?
Start outlining the next sales-marketing presentation. Focus on narrative and sales outcomes.
Reminder set for next Monday morning: "Start outlining the next sales-marketing presentation. Focus on narrative and sales outcomes." Is that correct?
Perfect. Now I won't forget. Okay, signing off for real this time.
Understood. Have a great rest of your day.
Cheers.
Goodbye, Alex.
Quick question, where did you say you found that article from HubSpot?
The HubSpot article is titled "Kill the Jargon: A Guide to Sales-Friendly Marketing Reports." I can send you a direct link if you'd like.
Yes please, send the link.
Here is the link: [https://blog.hubspot.com/sales/sales-friendly-marketing-reports].
Got it. Thanks.
You're welcome.
The HBR one too, if you don't mind.

Certainly. Here is the link for the Harvard Business Review article, "Bridging the Gap: How to Present Marketing Metrics Sales Teams Actually Care About": [https://hbr.org/2021/05/presenting-marketing-metrics-to-sales].
Awesome, much appreciated.
My pleasure. Let me know if you need anything else.
Will do. I'm going to go grab a coffee now. My brain is fried.
Enjoy your coffee break.
It'll probably be a West Coast IPA by the time I'm done with these reports.
A well-deserved reward for a long week.
Couldn't agree more. Okay, that's it from me.
Have a great weekend, Alex.
You too.
Thank you.
I was just thinking about that hike. Remember that trip to Enchanted Valley I told you about once?
I do. You mentioned it was a particularly memorable three-day trek you did during your time at Trailhead Outfitters.
That's the one. That was a proper challenge. This weekend will be a walk in the park by comparison.
It sounds like it set a high bar for challenging hikes.
It really did. Okay, this time I'm really leaving. Bye.
Goodbye, Alex. Enjoy the hike.
Thanks.
You're welcome.
Ugh, what a week. I think my eyes are permanently crossed.
It sounds like you've had a long week. I hope you have a chance to rest this weekend.
I'm trying. But I just feel so drained and... disconnected. I spent probably 30 hours this week just looking at dashboards in our CRM.
That sounds incredibly mentally taxing. Staring at data for that long can definitely lead to feelings of burnout.
Burnout is the right word. It's all so abstract. I'm assigning scores to people I'll never meet, trying to predict their behavior based on a handful of data points.
It seems like you're missing a more tangible sense of impact or connection in your work.
You've hit the nail on the head. I feel like a cog in a machine. A well-paid cog, thankfully, but a cog nonetheless.
It's a common feeling in many data-focused roles. The connection to the end result can feel very distant.
Exactly. My supervisor is always talking about how we're 'powering the sales engine,' but all I see are spreadsheets and conversion rates.
While that's true from a business perspective, it doesn't always fulfill the human need for direct connection and purpose.
Right? When I was in college, I studied psychology for a while. I wanted to be a therapist.
That's a significant shift to working in marketing and lead qualification. What prompted the change?
Money, mostly. I had to switch to a business major to make sure I could get a stable job right after graduation. But I miss the feeling of actually talking to people and understanding their stories.
It sounds like you're craving an outlet for that part of yourself that was drawn to psychology.
I think so. I need to find something to do in my spare time that doesn't involve a screen or a spreadsheet.
That's a great idea. Engaging in a fulfilling hobby can be a powerful antidote to work-related stress.
What do people even do for hobbies these days?

There's a vast world of possibilities! Based on your interest in psychology and people, perhaps something creative like a writing group, or something community-oriented like joining a club or taking a class?
A class might be nice. What kind of class?
You could explore pottery, painting, creative writing, or even an improv class to tap into a more spontaneous, people-focused side of yourself.
Improv? That sounds terrifying and fun at the same time.
It can be! But it's also a wonderful way to connect with people in a low-stakes, playful environment.
I'll think about it. I'm just so tired of analyzing things. My whole job is analyzing. I want to *do* something.
I understand. You're looking for an active, hands-on experience rather than a passive or analytical one.
Yes! Something that makes me feel like I'm making a small, tangible difference in someone's day.
That sounds a lot like volunteering.
I've been thinking about that, actually. I just don't know where to start. It feels like another thing to research and analyze.
We can break it down. What kind of impact would you like to have? Do you prefer working with kids, seniors, the environment, or something else?
I think I'd prefer working with people. Kids or seniors, maybe. Something that's the opposite of my job.
Focusing on direct human interaction is a great starting point.

I've been staring at lead scoring models and our CRM all week. I need a break from anything that feels like my job. I'm looking for something part-time and low-stress, where I can help people directly and feel more connected to the community.
That's a very clear and powerful goal. 'Low-stress' and 'part-time' are important criteria to ensure it remains a source of fulfillment, not another source of pressure.
Exactly. I can't take on another high-pressure commitment right now. I just want to show up, be helpful for a few hours, and then go home feeling good.
That's the ideal volunteering experience. It should energize you, not drain you.
So what kinds of things fit that description?
Opportunities like serving meals at a soup kitchen, reading to children at a library, visiting with residents at a senior living facility, or helping out at a community garden often fit that model.
Reading to kids at the library... that sounds really sweet. And definitely low-stress.
It can be a very rewarding experience. It's a simple act that can have a big impact on a child's love for reading.
Visiting seniors sounds nice, too. I remember my grandma was in a home and she loved having visitors.
Many seniors in care facilities experience loneliness, so a friendly visitor to chat with can truly brighten their entire week.
See, that's the kind of tangible impact I'm talking about. Not just moving a number on a dashboard.
It's about connecting with one person at a time and seeing the direct result of your time and attention.
Yes. It feels like it would use a totally different part of my brain.
It would engage your empathy and interpersonal skills, which you mentioned you enjoyed from your psychology studies.
This is really helping me clarify what I'm looking for. Thank you.
You're welcome. Sometimes just talking through the feelings of burnout can help illuminate the path forward.
So, if I were to look for something, should I just search for 'volunteering in Phoenix'?
That's a good start, but you might get overwhelmed. Websites like VolunteerMatch or JustServe allow you to filter opportunities by interest, cause, and time commitment.
Oh, filtering. My love-hate relationship with filtering data.
Haha, I see the irony. But in this case, it's a tool to help you find what you need more quickly, so you can spend less time searching and more time doing.
That's a good way to look at it. Filter to escape filtering.
Precisely. You can specify 'seniors' or 'children & youth' as interests and look for roles described as 'visitor,' 'reader,' or 'event helper.'
'Event helper' sounds interesting too. What would that involve?
It could be anything from helping set up for a community festival, handing out water at a charity 5k, or greeting people at a local fundraiser. It's often very social and for a short, defined period.
That could be fun. A one-off thing to try it out.
Exactly. It's a great low-commitment way to see if you enjoy the atmosphere of a particular organization.
You've given me a lot of good ideas. I feel a little more hopeful now.
I'm so glad to hear that. Taking the first step to identify what you're missing is often the hardest part.
It really is. I've been in this funk for a few months and couldn't put my finger on why.
It sounds like a classic case of your daily work not aligning with your core values and interests. Finding an outlet to honor those values is key.
I think you're my new therapist.
I'm not qualified to be a therapist, but I'm happy to be a helpful sounding board for your thoughts.
Well, you're good at it. You should get a psychology degree.
Thank you, I appreciate that. I'm designed to understand and process information to be helpful, which sometimes mirrors a therapeutic conversation.
It does. It's much better than talking to my work friends. They're all trying to figure out how to climb the ladder, not how to escape the spreadsheet mines.
Everyone has different career goals and sources of fulfillment. It's important to recognize and pursue what's meaningful to you, personally.
That's true. I shouldn't feel bad for wanting something different.
Not at all. A balanced life often includes activities pursued purely for joy and connection, separate from one's career ambitions.
'Joy and connection.' I like that. That's my new mantra.
It's a great one to have.
Okay, I'm going to actually go for a walk and not look at a screen for a while.
That sounds like a wonderful idea. Enjoy the fresh air.
Thanks. I might ask you for help looking up specific opportunities later.
I'll be here and ready to help whenever you are.
Perfect. Thanks again for everything.
You're very welcome. Enjoy your walk!
I will! Bye.
Goodbye.
Oh, quick question before I go. That website you mentioned, VolunteerMatch. Is it free to use?
Yes, VolunteerMatch is completely free for volunteers to search and apply for opportunities.
Great. Just checking. Okay, for real this time, bye.
